translatedData.title: Trading Discipline | Five Rules I Keep Beside My Screen—Sharing Them Just as They Are
translatedData.subTitle:
On emotional days, people forget every lesson, so I wrote these down and stuck them up:

1. Write down your stop-loss level before opening a position. If you can't write it down, don't open the position.
2. Never risk more than 2% of your capital on a single trade. No exceptions.
3. Never add to a losing position. Never average down.
4. After three consecutive losses, stop trading for the day. Just watch; don't trade.
5. Withdraw part of your profits. The money you take out is money; what you leave behind is peace of mind.

That's all five rules. Not one of them is about “how to read the market.” Because the reason people lose big money is never
that they misread the market; it's that their execution goes off track. Let's keep each other accountable.

The protocol automatically calculates the base fee based on usage in the previous block. If usage was above the target, the fee goes up; if it was below the target, the fee goes down.

translatedData.subTitle:
What is someone down 50% looking at? The “all-time high,” thinking: “If it gets back to my entry price,
I’ll get out.” Remember, this thought is all attachment and no logic. The market doesn’t know your entry price;
it only responds to current supply and demand.

Once you’re stuck holding a trade, you’ll automatically gather favorable news and filter out unfavorable news. This is called confirmation bias. You’ll think,
“This time is different.” Those five words have cost more money throughout history than any hacker ever has.

The remedy is actually simple, but hard to follow: before opening a position, write down “under what circumstances the logic behind this trade
will no longer hold,” then act when the time comes, regardless of how you feel. Separate your decisions from holding the position, and only then can you see clearly.
